children.title: Marcus Garvey & the UNIA Prosecution (1919–1927)
children.body:
Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association was the largest Black mass movement in American history — millions of members, the Black Star Line, and a program of African redemption that terrified the young J. Edgar Hoover, whose Bureau hired its first Black agents specifically to infiltrate it. Unable to find sedition, the government prosecuted Garvey in 1923 for mail fraud over a Black Star Line brochure — a case so thin it centered on a single empty envelope.

Sentenced to five years, Garvey entered Atlanta Penitentiary in 1925; President Coolidge commuted the sentence in 1927 on condition of deportation, and the movement's founder was shipped to Jamaica, never to return. The case established the template later perfected under COINTELPRO: when a Black movement cannot be defeated politically, imprison its leader on whatever charge can be made to stick.

children.title: RAM & the Early Black Power Prosecutions (1964–1968)
children.body:
Before the Panthers, the Revolutionary Action Movement — the clandestine organization around Max Stanford (Muhammad Ahmad), with Robert F. Williams as its exiled chairman — was the state's chief Black-revolutionary target. In 1967 police and the FBI announced they had foiled RAM plots to assassinate moderate leaders and poison Harlem's water: the "Queens 17" raids and the Herman Ferguson case, built on infiltrators whose stories the defense showed to be manufactured.

Ferguson, a respected assistant principal, was convicted of conspiracy in 1968 and jumped bail into two decades of exile rather than serve; on his 1989 return he served four years. The RAM cases — conspiracies proven by police agents, plots that never happened — rehearsed every technique of the COINTELPRO era on the movement's first revolutionary generation.

children.title: The COINTELPRO Frame-Ups (1968–1975)
children.body:
COINTELPRO's Black Nationalist Hate Groups program, ordered in 1967 to "prevent the rise of a messiah," worked through the courts as much as the streets. Geronimo ji-Jaga Pratt was convicted in 1972 of a murder the FBI's own wiretap logs showed he could not have committed — freed in 1997 after 27 years when the courts found the state had concealed that its star witness was a police and FBI informer. Dhoruba Bin Wahad served 19 years before disclosure of hidden files overturned his conviction in 1990; the Omaha Two, Ed Poindexter and Mondo we Langa, remained imprisoned for life on evidence their supporters and the Amnesty movement never stopped contesting.

The New York 21's acquittal in 1971 — after the longest political trial in the state's history collapsed under its own informers — showed what juries did when they saw the machinery plainly. The frame-up cases remain the heart of the American political-prisoner movement, several still unresolved after half a century.

children.title: The Mumia Abu-Jamal Case (1981– )
children.body:
Mumia Abu-Jamal — Black Panther Party veteran at fifteen, then Philadelphia's "voice of the voiceless" radio journalist and defender of MOVE — was convicted of the 1981 killing of Officer Daniel Faulkner and sentenced to death in a trial his supporters worldwide regard as the era's paradigmatic political proceeding: before Judge Albert Sabo, who a court stenographer swore she heard promise to help "fry the n----r," with a purged jury, suppressed witnesses, and a manufactured confession that surfaced months after the fact.

From death row Abu-Jamal became the world's best-known American political prisoner — author of Live from Death Row, honorary citizen of Paris, subject of protests on five continents. His death sentence was vacated in 2011 and he remains imprisoned for life without parole, his case still the dividing line in every argument over political imprisonment in the United States.

children.title: From Ferguson to the George Floyd Uprising: the New Prosecutions (2014– )
children.body:
The Movement for Black Lives brought the old machinery back under new names. After Ferguson, Josh Williams — nineteen years old — drew eight years for a QuikTrip fire, the uprising's longest sentence; the FBI minted a "Black Identity Extremist" category, and its first target, Rakem Balogun, was jailed months on gun charges built from his Facebook posts before a judge threw the case out. Activists like Jasmine Abdullah were convicted of "felony lynching" — the anti-mob statute inverted against Black protest.

The 2020 George Floyd uprising produced the largest protest prosecution wave in U.S. history: federal charges against hundreds, decades-long arson sentences, and cases — from the Grand Rapids and Little Rock defendants to New York's Urooj Rahman and Colinford Mattis — that the movement's lawyers organized to defend as political cases, reviving the mass-defense tradition of the Panther era.

children.title: The Dakota 38 & the Davenport Prisoners (1862–1866)
children.body:
After the U.S.–Dakota War of 1862 — the starvation-driven uprising in Minnesota — military commissions tried 392 Dakota men in proceedings lasting minutes each, without counsel, and condemned 303 to death. President Lincoln commuted most, but on December 26, 1862, thirty-eight Dakota men were hanged together at Mankato: the largest mass execution in American history, carried out the week of the Emancipation Proclamation.

The commuted and convicted — some 265 men — were shipped to a prison camp at Davenport, Iowa, where dozens died of disease over three years, while sixteen hundred Dakota women, children, and elders were interned at Fort Snelling and then exiled from Minnesota by act of Congress. The Dakota 38+2 memorial ride each December marks the case at the foundation of Indigenous political imprisonment.

children.title: Fort Marion, the Plains Prisoners & Geronimo's Apaches (1875–1913)
children.body:
In 1875, at the end of the Red River War, seventy-two Cheyenne, Kiowa, Comanche, and Arapaho men were chained into railcars and shipped to Fort Marion in St. Augustine, Florida — imprisoned without trial as hostages for their nations' good behavior. Their jailer's assimilation experiment (the prisoners' famous ledger art notwithstanding) became the model for the Carlisle boarding-school system: the prison as the laboratory of "killing the Indian to save the man."

A decade later the Chiricahua Apache — including the scouts who had served the Army — were deported wholesale to Florida when Geronimo surrendered in 1886. Geronimo and his people remained prisoners of war for twenty-seven years, dying in the damp casemates of Fort Pickens and Mount Vernon Barracks and finally at Fort Sill, where Geronimo died still a POW in 1909; the survivors were released only in 1913.

children.title: The Fish Wars: Billy Frank Jr. & the Fish-Ins (1954–1974)
children.body:
In the rivers of Washington State, treaty fishing became the crime of the century's midpoint. Nisqually fisherman Billy Frank Jr. was first arrested at fourteen, in 1945, and more than fifty times thereafter for exercising rights his nation had reserved in the Treaty of Medicine Creek; through the 1960s the "fish-ins" at Frank's Landing — joined by Puyallup leaders like Ramona Bennett and celebrities like Marlon Brando and Dick Gregory, who served time in Thurston County jail — met state game wardens' clubs, boats rammed, nets confiscated, families beaten on the riverbank.

The campaign of deliberate arrest, modeled consciously on the southern sit-ins, produced its vindication in 1974: United States v. Washington, the Boldt decision, affirmed the tribes' right to half the salmon harvest and made the fish-in defendants the authors of modern treaty law.

children.title: Alcatraz & the Red Power Occupations (1969–1975)
children.body:
On November 20, 1969, Indians of All Tribes landed on Alcatraz Island and claimed the abandoned prison "by right of discovery," offering the government twenty-four dollars in glass beads and red cloth for it. The nineteen-month occupation — led at first by Richard Oakes, with LaNada War Jack, John Trudell's Radio Free Alcatraz, and hundreds of residents — was the founding act of Red Power, ended by federal removal in June 1971.

Alcatraz begat a wave of occupations — Fort Lawton (where Bernie Whitebear's occupiers were jailed and won the land that became Daybreak Star), Mount Rushmore, the BIA building, and dozens more — whose arrestees were the movement's first cohort of prisoners. The occupations' veterans built the American Indian Movement's national campaigns, traced in this section's AIM pages.

children.title: Standing Rock & the Water Protector Prosecutions (2016–2018)
children.body:
The #NoDAPL encampments at Standing Rock — the largest Indigenous gathering in a century — were met with a militarized response run jointly by the state, National Guard, and the pipeline company's TigerSwan mercenaries: water cannon in freezing temperatures, dog attacks, and more than 800 criminal cases against water protectors, coordinated through a private-public fusion apparatus later exposed in leaked documents.

Red Fawn Fallis, whose boyfriend proved to be a paid FBI informant who owned the gun in her case, served years in federal prison as the prosecutions' central political prisoner; Michael "Little Feather" Giron and Michael "Rattler" Markus took federal civil-disorder pleas. The mass-defense project that fought the 800 cases — winning dismissal or acquittal in the great majority — carried the fish-in and Wounded Knee legal traditions into the pipeline era, from Standing Rock to Line 3 and Mauna Kea.

children.title: El Grito de Lares & the First Political Prisoners (1868)
children.body:
The Puerto Rican independence tradition dates its calendar from September 23, 1868, when hundreds of rebels organized by Ramón Emeterio Betances proclaimed the Republic of Puerto Rico in the mountain town of Lares before Spanish forces crushed the rising. Some 475 rebels were imprisoned in Arecibo and Aguadilla, where dozens died of yellow fever in the crowded cells before an 1869 amnesty freed the survivors.

Lares gave the movement its flag, its martyrs, and its anniversary — the date on which the Macheteros' founder Filiberto Ojeda Ríos would be killed by the FBI 137 years later. Every subsequent generation of independence prisoners, under Spain and then under the United States, has claimed the lineage of Lares.

children.title: Vieques: the Navy, the Fishermen & the Mass Arrests (1978–2003)
children.body:
The Navy's use of Vieques as a live-fire range made the island municipality the independence movement's great unifying cause. The fishermen's blockades of 1978–79 brought the first wave of prosecutions: twenty-one protesters arrested on the range in May 1979 included Ángel Rodríguez Cristóbal of the Socialist League, who was found hanged in his cell at the federal prison in Tallahassee that November — a death the movement has always counted a murder, answered by the Macheteros at Sabana Seca.

After stray bombs killed civilian guard David Sanes in April 1999, civil disobedience became general: encampments on the range, and upon their removal a four-year campaign in which more than 1,500 people were arrested, from Rubén Berríos and island legislators to Al Sharpton and Robert Kennedy Jr., many serving federal sentences at Guaynabo. The Navy left Vieques on May 1, 2003 — the movement's clearest victory, won by filling the jails.

children.title: The Grand Jury Resisters (1976–2011)
children.body:
From the mid-1970s the government wielded the federal grand jury against the independence movement's aboveground supporters — subpoenaing organizers, churchworkers, and family members to testify about the FALN and Macheteros, and jailing those who refused for civil and criminal contempt. María Cueto and Raisa Nemikin of the Episcopal Church's Hispanic commission served ten months in 1977; a 1983 wave imprisoned Julio Rosado and his brothers; in all, dozens of independentistas — and their North American allies — served terms without ever being accused of a crime.

The movement built noncollaboration into a principle: the resisters were honored as prisoners of the same war, and the tactic's costs fell on the state as refusals held. Grand juries returned in 2000s Hartford and as late as 2011 against aging Macheteros supporters — met by the same refusal, now three generations deep.

children.title: The Clemency Campaigns: 1979, 1999 & Oscar López (1977–2017)
children.body:
Three times the movement has freed its prisoners through mass campaigns rather than courts. In 1979 President Carter commuted the sentences of the four Nationalist prisoners of 1950–54 — Lolita Lebrón, Rafael Cancel Miranda, Irvin Flores, and Oscar Collazo — after a worldwide campaign in which the prisoners refused to request clemency themselves. In 1999 President Clinton, pressed by a coalition running from the churches to Coretta Scott King and Desmond Tutu, freed eleven FALN prisoners and cut Juan Segarra Palmer's term, over the objection of Congress and the FBI.

Oscar López Rivera, who refused the 1999 offer's conditions while co-defendants walked, became the campaign's final cause: 35 years served, twelve in Marion and ADX isolation, until President Obama commuted his sentence in January 2017 and San Juan received him — the last of the era's Puerto Rican political prisoners — with a hero's welcome.

children.title: Las Carpetas: the Surveillance State (1936–1999)
children.body:
Behind every prosecution stood the archive. For six decades the insular police's intelligence division, in partnership with the FBI, maintained carpetas — dossiers — on independence supporters: some 135,000 people ultimately had files, built by neighbors, coworkers, and informers, used to deny jobs, licenses, and peace to anyone touched by independentismo. The Cerro Maravilla killings of 1978, in which police executed two young independentistas delivered by an agent provocateur, showed the machinery's lethal end.

In 1988 the Puerto Rico Supreme Court declared the system unconstitutional and ordered the files delivered to their subjects — hundreds of thousands of pages that documented, in the state's own hand, the criminalization of a political ideal. The carpetas' release, and the FBI's parallel disclosure of over 1.8 million pages after 2000, made Puerto Rico the best-documented case of political policing in American history.

children.title: The Golden Rule & the Test-Ban Voyages (1958–1962)
children.body:
In 1958 Albert Bigelow, a former Navy commander turned Quaker pacifist, sailed the thirty-foot ketch Golden Rule toward the Marshall Islands to place his body inside the H-bomb test zone. Arrested twice in Honolulu with his crew and jailed sixty days for trying, Bigelow inspired the Phoenix of Hiroshima to complete the voyage into the zone weeks later — earning its skipper Earle Reynolds a federal conviction, later overturned.

The voyages, organized with the new Committee for Non-Violent Action, invented the template of direct interposition that Greenpeace would later make famous, and their jailed crews were the first prisoners of the anti-nuclear cause. CNVA's land campaigns — trespasses at Cheyenne's missile fields and the Omaha Action of 1959, where the elderly A.J. Muste climbed the fence — carried the same witness to the weapons themselves.

children.title: Seabrook & the Clamshell Alliance (1976–1978)
children.body:
The Clamshell Alliance's campaign against the Seabrook nuclear plant on the New Hampshire coast created the modern mass-action model: affinity groups, consensus decision-making, and nonviolence trainings borrowed from the civil-rights movement. On April 30–May 1, 1977, over two thousand occupied the site; 1,414 were arrested — and when they refused bail solidarity, Governor Meldrim Thomson held them two weeks in National Guard armories, an improvised mass imprisonment that became a school of the movement.

The armory fortnight — meetings, trainings, and songs under guard — welded a generation of organizers and spread the Clamshell model to the Abalone, Shad, and Catfish alliances nationwide. Seabrook's second reactor was never built; the first opened over a decade late, into an industry the occupations had helped halt at 100-odd cancelled plants.

children.title: Diablo Canyon & the Abalone Alliance Blockade (1977–1984)
children.body:
California's Abalone Alliance carried the Clamshell model to the Diablo Canyon plant, built beside an earthquake fault near San Luis Obispo. The September 1981 blockade — two weeks of affinity-group waves by land and sea from the Rachel Carson — produced over 1,900 arrests, the largest number in the history of American anti-nuclear action; Jackson Browne went to jail alongside grandmothers from the Mothers for Peace, the plant's original church-basement opponents.

Days after the blockade ended, PG&E admitted its seismic blueprints had been reversed between the plant's twin units — vindicating the blockaders as the licensing collapsed into years of rework. Diablo opened anyway in 1985, but the Abalone campaign's fifty-plus affinity-group culture became the organizing DNA of the decade's disarmament and Central America movements.

children.title: Rocky Flats: the Tracks Blockades (1978–1989)
children.body:
At the Rocky Flats plant outside Denver — where every American plutonium trigger was made — the movement put its bodies on the railroad. Beginning in April 1978, blockaders occupied the tracks into the plant for over a year; among the hundreds arrested were Daniel Ellsberg and the poet Allen Ginsberg, whose "Plutonian Ode" was written the night before his arrest. The trials became forums on the bomb, with defendants arguing necessity to Colorado juries.

The campaign built the coalition of pacifists, downwinders, and eventually plant workers whose pressure — joined in 1989 by an unprecedented FBI raid on the plant itself for environmental crimes — closed Rocky Flats for good: a rare case in which the protesters' indictment of a facility was ratified by the government's own.

children.title: The Nevada Test Site & the Desert Witness (1982–1994)
children.body:
The Nevada Desert Experience's Lenten vigils at the nuclear test site drew what became the largest sustained civil-disobedience campaign in American history: between 1986 and 1994, more than 15,000 arrests at the cattle guard on Mercury Highway, with single actions — the Mothers' Day and "Reclaim the Test Site" gatherings of 1987–88 — producing one and two thousand arrests at a time. Franciscans and Shoshone elders, physicists and celebrities (Martin Sheen, repeatedly; Carl Sagan, twice) cycled through the Beatty and Tonopah jails.

The Western Shoshone National Council issued permits to the trespassers — the land, under the Treaty of Ruby Valley, being theirs — turning every arrest into a sovereignty case. When the United States halted full-scale testing in 1992, the desert campaign, with the downwinders and the global test-ban movement, had made the moratorium politically irreversible.

children.title: The Plowshares Tradition (1980– )
children.body:
On September 9, 1980, eight Catholic radicals led by Daniel and Philip Berrigan walked into the General Electric plant at King of Prussia, Pennsylvania, hammered on Mark 12A warhead nose cones, and poured their blood on the weapons — enacting Isaiah's command to beat swords into plowshares. The Plowshares Eight received prison terms after a trial (dramatized with the defendants themselves in In the King of Prussia) that launched a tradition: over a hundred such actions worldwide since.

American Plowshares prisoners span four decades — from Helen Woodson's seventeen-plus years, the tradition's longest, through the Transform Now trio whose 82-year-old Sister Megan Rice reached the heart of the Y-12 uranium complex in 2012, to the Kings Bay Plowshares 7 of 2018. The full tradition has its own page under Categories → Civil Disobedience & Plowshares; it stands here as the anti-nuclear movement's most sustained prisoner witness.

children.title: World War I: the Espionage Act & the Conscientious Objectors (1917–1921)
children.body:
The First World War produced America's first mass political imprisonment of the modern era: over two thousand prosecutions under the Espionage and Sedition Acts for speeches, articles, and leaflets against the war — Eugene Debs sentenced to ten years for a single speech at Canton, Ohio, and running for president from Atlanta Penitentiary with nearly a million votes; Kate Richards O'Hare, Rose Pastor Stokes, and the Socialist and IWW press swept wholesale into the courts.

Alongside them stood some 500 absolutist conscientious objectors court-martialed into Leavenworth and Alcatraz, where they were shackled to cell bars and fed bread and water; the Hutterite Hofer brothers died from their treatment at Leavenworth in 1918. The COs' prison strikes and the amnesty campaign that finally freed Debs in 1921 built the organizations — the ACLU first among them — that every later antiwar generation would inherit.

children.title: World War II: the Prison Strikes of the COs (1940–1946)
children.body:
Nearly six thousand conscientious objectors went to federal prison during the Second World War — one in six federal prisoners by war's end — most of them Jehovah's Witnesses, alongside the radical pacifists whose draft-card refusals put them in Danbury, Lewisburg, and Ashland. Inside, they turned the prisons into laboratories of nonviolence: the Danbury strike of 1943 desegregated the dining hall after 135 days, and hunger strikes by Stanley Murphy and Louis Taylor at Lewisburg lasted into forced-feeding for over a year.

The war's CO prisoners — Bayard Rustin, David Dellinger, Ralph DiGia, Bill Sutherland among them — carried prison-tested tactics directly into the postwar movements: Rustin from a Kentucky cellblock to the March on Washington, Dellinger to the Chicago conspiracy dock. Their strikes were the first sustained direct-action assault on prison segregation anywhere in America.

children.title: Vietnam: Draft Resistance & the Draft-Board Raids (1964–1973)
children.body:
The Vietnam draft resistance filled the federal prisons a third time: over 200,000 men were reported for draft offenses, some 3,250 imprisoned — David Harris among the most famous — while David Miller's 1965 card-burning tested the new mutilation law and Dr. Spock and the Boston Five were tried for conspiracy for supporting them. Muhammad Ali's refusal — "no Viet Cong ever called me n----r" — cost him his title and nearly his freedom until the Supreme Court reversed in 1971.

The Catholic left escalated from refusing the draft to destroying it: the Baltimore Four poured blood on the files in 1967, the Catonsville Nine burned 378 files with homemade napalm in 1968 — Daniel Berrigan's "apologies, good friends, for the fracture of good order" — and dozens of raids followed, until the Camden 28's 1973 acquittal, by a jury told the FBI had built the raid through its informer, effectively ended the prosecutions.

children.title: The GI Movement: Resistance Inside the Military (1966–1972)
children.body:
The war was also refused from inside the ranks. The Fort Hood Three went to Leavenworth in 1966 for refusing Vietnam orders; Captain Howard Levy was court-martialed in 1967 for refusing to train Green Beret medics; and after the Presidio 27 sat down and sang "We Shall Overcome" over the guard-shooting of a fellow stockade prisoner in 1968, the Army charged them with mutiny — seeking, initially, terms up to sixteen years for singing. Black GIs bore the heaviest hand: the Fort Hood 43, who refused Chicago riot duty in 1968, and men like Billy Dean Smith, held for a fragging he was acquitted of.

With coffeehouses ringing the bases, over 200 underground GI papers, and desertion at historic highs, the movement in uniform — punished through stockades from the Presidio to Long Binh Jail — did as much as any civilian campaign to make the war unsustainable.

children.title: The Long War: Resisters from the Gulf to the Drone Era (1991– )
children.body:
Each American war since has renewed the tradition. The Gulf War jailed refusers like Marine corporal Jeff Paterson, who sat down on the tarmac; the Iraq War produced Camilo Mejía, the first combat veteran imprisoned for refusing to return, Kevin Benderman, Agustín Aguayo — and Lt. Ehren Watada, the first officer to refuse deployment, whose court-martial ended in mistrial and discharge. Kathleen Gilberd's and the GI-rights movement's counseling networks revived the Vietnam infrastructure for a volunteer military.

Civilian resistance ran through Voices in the Wilderness — Kathy Kelly repeatedly imprisoned, from sanctions-breaking flights to Baghdad to walking onto drone bases — the SOA Watch line-crossers at Fort Benning, and the Hancock and Beale drone-base defendants of the 2010s: the whole apparatus of the era's wars met, action by action, with the same willingness to go to jail that began at Canton, Ohio in 1918.

children.title: Earth First!, Redwood Summer & the Judi Bari Bombing (1985–2002)
children.body:
Earth First! brought civil disobedience into the ancient forests — tree-sits, road blockades, and the mass trespasses of the 1990 Redwood Summer campaign against liquidation logging of California's redwoods. Its organizers paid in arrests by the hundred and worse: on May 24, 1990, a pipe bomb exploded under the car seat of Redwood Summer's lead organizer Judi Bari, shattering her pelvis. Within hours the FBI and Oakland police arrested Bari and Darryl Cherney — the victims — for transporting the bomb, and fed the press the movement-as-terrorist story while making no serious effort to find the bomber.

Charges were dropped for the absence of any evidence, and in 2002 a federal jury awarded Bari's estate and Cherney $4.4 million, finding FBI agents and Oakland officers had violated their civil rights — the environmental movement's own COINTELPRO verdict, delivered five years after Bari's death.

children.title: Tree-Sits, Forest Defense & the Pain-Compliance Era (1995–2002)
children.body:
The late-1990s forest-defense campaigns — Warner Creek's eleven-month blockade, Julia Butterfly Hill's two years aloft in Luna, the Fall Creek and Headwaters actions — made the occupied tree the movement's signature and the county jail its common experience. Police answered lockdowns with "pain compliance": in 1997 Humboldt deputies swabbed pepper spray directly into the eyes of locked-down Headwaters protesters, video that shocked the country and produced a federal jury verdict against the county in 2005.

The era's martyr was David "Gypsy" Chain, killed in 1998 by a tree felled by an enraged Pacific Lumber logger — no charges were brought. The forest campaigns' veterans, criminalized in the woods, supplied both the aboveground movement's organizers and, when legal routes seemed exhausted, the clandestine cells whose story is told in this section's ELF pages.

children.title: The Valve Turners & the Climate Necessity Defense (2016–2018)
children.body:
On October 11, 2016, five climate activists simultaneously closed the emergency valves on the five pipelines carrying Canadian tar-sands oil into the United States — Ken Ward, Emily Johnston, Annette Klapstein, Leonard Higgins, and Michael Foster, with their support crews — then waited to be arrested, in order to put the climate emergency itself on trial. Foster served six months in North Dakota; the others faced years-long maximums across four states.

Their cases turned the necessity defense into the movement's courtroom: a Minnesota court allowed expert climate testimony before acquitting Johnston and Klapstein outright, and Ward's Washington juries refused to convict on the felony. The valve turners — grandparents, retired attorneys, a pediatrician — normalized the proposition their trials argued: that in a physical emergency the law's presumptions reverse.

children.title: Pipeline Sabotage & the Terrorism Enhancement: Reznicek & Montoya (2016–2021)
children.body:
Catholic Workers Jessica Reznicek and Ruby Montoya spent 2016–17 burning heavy equipment and torching valve sites along the Dakota Access pipeline in Iowa, then publicly confessed at a press conference and awaited prosecution — sabotage in the Plowshares idiom, harming no one. In 2021 Reznicek was sentenced to eight years with a domestic-terrorism enhancement — the same instrument used on the Green Scare defendants — a designation affirmed on appeal despite briefs from civil-liberties groups across the spectrum; Montoya received six years.

The cases fixed the era's asymmetry in a single frame: the pipeline's spills drew fines, while the women who damaged its machinery in protest were sentenced as terrorists. "Water is life," Reznicek said at sentencing; her case became the successor cause of the eco-prisoner movement as the Green Scare generation came home.

children.title: Stop Cop City: Domestic Terrorism & RICO for a Forest (2021– )
children.body:
The campaign to stop Atlanta's police-training center — Cop City — in the Weelaunee Forest brought every prior instrument together: dozens of forest defenders charged with domestic terrorism under Georgia law, many on evidence as thin as mud on their shoes; the January 2023 police killing of Manuel "Tortuguita" Terán, shot at least 57 times in their tent during a raid, with body cameras off; and bail-fund organizers arrested for charity fraud over reimbursing protest supplies.

In September 2023 Georgia's attorney general indicted 61 people under the state RICO statute — treating the entire movement, from tree-sitters to legal observers to zine distributors, as a criminal enterprise, in the broadest conspiracy prosecution ever aimed at American environmentalism. The case, still unfolding, has made "Cop City" the emblem of the new era in which protest infrastructure itself is prosecuted.
